1	# Biên kịch — luật làm truyện của kênh (Mốc B, 05/10/2026)
2	
3	WRITER đọc file này **trước** khi viết treatment hoặc kịch bản (`episode.md` §3). Gom từ `genre-spec/data-explainer.md` §3–4 (DX-S1…S11, DX-R1…R6), sổ gu G-007/008/009/013, ba tham chiếu (`references.md`) và số đo Tập 1–3 (`lessons.md` F2, F3). File này chỉ có luật, **không có câu mẫu**: cold open mỗi tập viết mới từ sự thật của tập đó.
4	
5	## 1. Móc: 30 giây đầu
6	1. **5 s đầu** là một trong hai thứ, dựa trên **sự thật hiện tại** (có claim, có ngày):
7	   - **được–mất:** một người như người xem đang được hay mất một khoản cụ thể;
8	   - **câu hỏi của người xem:** câu họ tự hỏi khi đứng trước quyết định này.
9	   Không mở bằng định nghĩa, lịch sử hay phương pháp. (Tập 3: câu hỏi đầu tiên đến ở 0:37.)
10	2. **Lời hứa cụ thể trước 0:30**: người xem sẽ biết điều gì, đo được, và tập giữ đúng lời hứa đó (DX-S4, G-013: một ngưỡng tự đối chiếu được).
11	3. **Ràng buộc claim-risk đặt SAU móc, không trước.** Giả định, phạm vi, "US only" nói ngay sau lời hứa, trước số lịch sử đầu tiên. Không chen vào giữa câu hỏi và lời hứa. (Tập 3: 22 s ràng buộc chen giữa hai câu này.)
12	4. Người trước số: một người và một khoảnh khắc cụ thể (G-007), bối cảnh đủ để hiểu vì sao người đó đứng trước quyết định (G-009). Được dùng một câu bối cảnh ngắn **trước** nhân vật nếu thiếu nó người xem không hiểu.
13	5. **Ba phương án móc:** ở P1, WRITER viết 3 phương án cho 30 s đầu, mỗi phương án một kiểu móc khác nhau (`packaging.md` §2). Cách chọn ở `episode.md` §3.
14	
15	## 2. Xương truyện
16	- **Chuỗi:** bối cảnh → nhân vật → vấn đề → hành trình → đáp án → giới hạn (G-009). Câu chữ liền mạch, có chuyển ý; không đưa số khi người xem chưa biết vì sao cần nó.
17	- **Mỗi hồi có một câu hỏi và một điểm vỡ lẽ.** Câu hỏi đặt ở đầu hồi. Điểm vỡ lẽ là lúc hình và lời cùng làm người xem đổi cách nghĩ. Hồi 3 trả lời đúng câu hỏi của cold open, gọi lại bằng cùng hình hoặc cùng chữ, rồi nói ngay giới hạn (DX-S2, DX-S3).
18	- **Con số cốt lõi quay lại ≥ 3 lần, mỗi lần mang nghĩa mới**: lần đầu là sự kiện; lần sau là so sánh; lần cuối là ngưỡng cho người xem. Lần nhắc lại gọi bằng lời, không đọc lại số (DX-S6, lessons E5).
19	- **Cái giá cụ thể:** năm, số dư, thực hay danh nghĩa; mọi điểm quyết định gọi tên năm và số dư (DX-S5, G-008).
20	- **Câu đối trọng** sau mỗi kết luận, chặn suy diễn "X tốt hơn"; không mệnh lệnh với người xem (lessons E4).
21	
22	## 2b. Cảm xúc: năm luật nhân vật (tổng kết Tập 5 §2b, chủ dự án duyệt 08/10)
23	Tập 5: đạo diễn máy A chấm cảm xúc 2 — lý do chỉ thẳng vào kịch bản: người xem chỉ được gọi là "you" ở S01 rồi 4 phút luật không có người; ba người mua hứa ở S03.4 mà 4,5 phút sau mới có tên; câu ở đỉnh cảm xúc (Victor, S17.3) dài và rối nhất; kết bằng câu khái quát.
24	1. **Một nhân vật dẫn đường từ cold open đến kết** (người điển hình): xuất hiện trước 0:45 (M5), đi qua phần phương pháp (vd "Grace's month is one of 307"), và **câu kết là câu của chính người đó**. Các nhân vật khác là đối trọng, ra ở hồi 3.
25	2. **Lời hứa nhân vật phải trả trong ≤ 90 s**, hoặc không hứa (điều kiện móc **M6**, `episode.md` §3.9).
26	3. **Cái được–mất bằng vật cụ thể khi không được nêu số tiền:** số hoá đơn, số tháng, một vật trong thế giới 3D (chồng tiền mệnh giá cố định) — "23 more bills" thay cho "$X". Vật và số vẫn phải có claim.
27	4. **Câu ở đỉnh cảm xúc ≤ 15 từ, một ý một câu** (REVIEWER soát ở C2; Victor S17.3 Tập 5 là ví dụ trượt).
28	5. **Kết quay về câu hỏi của nhân vật dẫn đường**, không quay về khái quát.
29	Nhân vật minh hoạ vẫn mang nhãn ILLUSTRATIVE ở mọi khung (gen được bảo vệ). Cảm xúc không đo bằng máy: thước là phiếu L3 dòng 1; đạo diễn máy chỉ chẩn đoán. Nhân vật dẫn đường làm `101` dài thêm ≈ 15–25 s — tính vào ước độ dài (§2c, `check_script.py`), không độn.
30	
31	## 3. Nhịp: mật độ số và khoảng thở
32	- **≤ 1 số mới mỗi ~8 s; không cảnh nào > 2 số mới** (DX-S7). Đoạn có ≥ 3 số liền nhau thì đưa bớt lên hình. Kiểm trước khi sinh giọng.
33	- **Sau mỗi số quyết định: ≥ 1 s không lời** (DX-R3), cùng ≥ 3 khoảng lặng có chủ ý 0,8–1,5 s trong tập (DX-R6).
34	- Câu ngắn xen câu dài (DX-S8). Mỗi hồi có một đỉnh căng, sau đó là khoảng nghỉ (DX-R1). Không đoạn nào > 60 s mà không đổi hình hay lớp âm (DX-R2).
35	- Đoạn phương pháp = 1 câu lời + thẻ phương pháp + mô tả (thư viện hình V7).
36	
37	## 4. Khuôn tỉ lệ thời lượng (G-009) — THAM KHẢO
38	Đích tính theo % thời lượng tập. Phần nào **lệch > ±5 điểm %** thì nêu tên trong báo cáo C2; không phải ngưỡng chặn.
39	
40	| Phần | `lab` (9–11 phút) | `101` (8–9 phút) |
41	|---|---|---|
42	| Móc + lời hứa + ràng buộc | 8 % (≤ 0:50) | 8 % |
43	| Bối cảnh và nhân vật / khái niệm | 15 % | 25 % (khái niệm) |
44	| Hành trình (phép thử trên dữ liệu thật) | 45 % | 30 % (thí nghiệm nhỏ) |
45	| Đáp án + ngưỡng cho người xem / khác nhau ở 2–3 người | 20 % | 25 % (2–3 người) |
46	| Giới hạn + thẻ phương pháp + outro | 12 % | 12 % (giới hạn) |
47	
48	**`101` không độn nội dung:** không đủ chất thì ngắn hơn hoặc gộp khái niệm; thời lượng tối thiểu không bao giờ là lý do thêm câu.
49	
50	## 5. Điểm chèn quảng cáo (mid-roll)
51	- Chỉ đặt ở **ranh giới hồi**, trong khoảng lặng tự nhiên ≥ 1 s (DX-S10).
52	- **Không đặt trong 2 phút đầu hay 2 phút cuối.**
53	- `lab`: 2 điểm; `101`: 1 điểm. Ghi mốc trong `episode.yaml` (`midrolls`).
54	
55	## 6. Đo bằng gì
56	- Ở C2, máy kiểm mật độ số, khoảng thở, mốc lời hứa (< 0:30), khuôn tỉ lệ (Tham khảo). Kiểm mù lời theo `quality-framework.md` §4.
57	- **Điểm móc 1–5 và "bỏ xem ở đâu" của agent: KHÔNG dùng** (hiệu chuẩn Mốc B trượt, lessons F3). So cặp móc chỉ dùng sau hiệu chuẩn chính thức ở P1 Tập 4.
58	- **Thước đo thật là giữ chân YouTube** (`audience.md`): điểm rời lớn nhất → nhịp kịch bản tương ứng → sửa file này.

Nhân vật minh hoạ vẫn mang nhãn ILLUSTRATIVE ở mọi khung (gen được bảo vệ). Cảm xúc không đo bằng máy: thước là phiếu L3 dòng 1; đạo diễn máy chỉ chẩn đoán. Nhân vật dẫn đường làm `101` dài thêm ≈ 15–25 s — tính vào ước độ dài (§2c, `check_script.py`), không độn.

## 4. Khuôn tỉ lệ thời lượng (G-009) — THAM KHẢO

1	# Claim — Tập 7 (Việc 0; claim ID = khoá `quantities` của `out/model.json`)
2	
3	Dữ liệu (FRED, tải 2026-10-11, `data/fetch.py`; không commit): MORTGAGE30US + MORTGAGE15US (Freddie Mac PMMS, tuần) → **1.833 tuần ghép, 1991-08-30 → 2026-10-08**. Đối chiếu Optimal Blue OBMMIC30YF/OBMMIC15YF (trung bình 7 ngày, từ 2017): **510/510 tuần trong 0,5 điểm** cho cả hai (lệch lớn nhất 0,384 / 0,282). Bản ghim hồ sơ `topics-r2/machine/debt-1/sources.json` (coed=2026-09-24): **SHA khớp**, tiền tố tệp mới trùng, +2 tuần.
4	Tính: `model/model.py` (từ định nghĩa hồ sơ, không gọi calc.py). calc.py hồ sơ trên bản ghim: **18/18 trùng `result.json`**; trên dữ liệu mới: số "hiện tại" đổi theo tuần 2026-10-08 (7,40 % / 6,73 %). 9	- No advice ("take the 15-year", "always prepay"). Show the dollar cost next to the flexibility.

11

13	- Weekly survey averages for prime borrowers with about 20% down; points and fees differ by term and lender.
14	- Payments are principal and interest only; no taxes, insurance, discounting or investing of differences.
15	- The value of the flexibility (job loss, emergencies) is not measured.

- A buyer in a high-cost metro area with a large monthly payment and little room in the budget, wondering whether a 15-year payoff is realistic and how to handle PMI or escrowed taxes first.
- A veteran or near-retiree with a VA or other government-backed loan who wants to be debt free before retiring, while still paying heavy state and local property taxes.

## Điểm yếu đối thủ (khán giả phàn nàn / máy thấy)
- Treats early payoff as the default best choice and gives little weight to opportunity cost, investment returns, or liquidity.
- Assumes viewers can easily afford large extra payments and rarely shows how to plan around tight budgets or high-cost housing.
- Glosses over differences between loan types (FHA mortgage insurance, VA rules), escrow, and property taxes, so the numbers may not apply to everyone.

**L1:** This week, a buyer borrowing $320,000 can take a 15-year mortgage at 6.73%, or a 30-year at 7.40% and pay it off in 15 years anyway, keeping the lower required payment as a fallback. We replay every week of US mortgage rates since 1991 to put a dollar price on that fallback, and to show what each extra dollar of principal actually earns: the bar any other use of that money has to clear. History, not a forecast: it won't tell you which loan to take, or whether to invest.

**L2 (phương án):** Pay extra on the mortgage, or invest the difference? Each extra dollar of principal earns exactly the loan's rate, so the answer starts with that rate. We follow a buyer borrowing $320,000 this week who can take a 15-year loan at 6.73%, or a 30-year at 7.40% paid off in 15 years, and replay every week of US mortgage rates since 1991: what the 30-year's lower fallback payment has cost, and how high the prepayment bar has been. # Thư viện hình của kênh (v1, 04/10/2026)

Gom từ Tập 1–2 những ký hiệu **đã qua kiểm mù**. Từ Tập 3, C3 dựng **một hướng** từ thư viện này và chỉ thiết kế mới cho nhịp chưa có ký hiệu (`playbook/quality-framework.md` v2 §4). Chủ dự án có quyền yêu cầu thêm hướng ở C3.

Mã ở đây là **mã tham chiếu** chép từ tập gốc (CHARTER §3.1: đồ dùng một lần). Tập mới chép sang thư mục của tập rồi sửa; không sửa tại chỗ. Số trên hình luôn qua `CL(claimId)`.

## 1. Nền chung

109	def words_int(n):
110	    if n < 20:
111	        return 1
112	    if n < 100:
113	        return 1
114	    if n < 1000:

# Script — Episode 7 (format `lab`, C2 v1, WRITER, 2026-10-11)

(header filled after the checker run)

---

=== COLD OPEN ===

## S01 — Tessa's fallback has a price

S01.1 {hook} Tessa's mortgage fallback costs $120 a month. <!-- claims: extra_vs15_month_now -->
S01.2 {hook} She's borrowing $320,000 this week, and in her city that payment is already her biggest bill. <!-- claims: interest_15_now, last_week -->

## S02 — Her question, and the promise

S02.1 {question} [curious] A 15-year mortgage, or a 30-year she pays off in 15 years anyway, with its lower payment kept for a bad month? <!-- claims: pay30on15_now -->
S02.2 {promise} We replayed every week the US survey priced both loans, to put that fallback in dollars, and to find what each extra dollar of principal earns. <!-- claims: n_weeks; hold: 0.5 -->

## S03 — Who Tessa is, this week's rates, the limits (shared continuation for all three hooks)

S03.1 {hook} Tessa is illustrative, but her rates are real: this week's survey has the 15-year at 6.73 percent and the 30-year at 7.40. <!-- claims: r15_now, r30_now -->
S03.2 {constraint} This is US only, and it's history, not a forecast. <!-- claims: — -->
S03.3 {constraint} It won't say which loan to take, or whether to invest. <!-- claims: —; hold: 0.8 -->

=== IDENT (3 s, no narration) ===

=== ACT 1 — CONTEXT: two loans, one fallback, and what it costs Tessa ===

## S04 — Two payments

S04.1 {hook} Here is what Tessa is weighing. <!-- claims: — -->
S04.2 On $320,000, the 15-year loan's payment is $2,828 a month. <!-- claims: pay15_now, interest_15_now -->
S04.3 The 30-year loan only requires $2,216. <!-- claims: pay30_now; hold: 0.8 -->

## S05 — The fallback

S05.1 That gap, about $613 a month, is the fallback: in a tight month, it's the least the 30-year asks of her. <!-- claims: fallback_gap_now; hold: 1.0 -->
S05.2 The bigger payment fits her budget today, but only just, and a job change or a repair could squeeze it. <!-- claims: — -->
S05.3 Still, she wants the house paid off in 15 years, so the 30-year only works for her if she pays it like a short loan. <!-- claims: pay30on15_now -->

## S06 — The price of paying the 30-year in 15

S06.1 At 7.40 percent, finishing that loan in 15 years takes $2,948 a month. <!-- claims: pay30on15_now, r30_now -->
S06.2 That's $120 a month more than the 15-year loan, for the same house and the same 15 years. <!-- claims: extra_vs15_month_now, pay30on15_now -->
S06.3 Over those 15 years, the extra adds up to $21,622. <!-- claims: extra_vs15_total_now; hold: 1.2 -->

## S07 — The stack

S07.1 Picture it as a stack of bills beside her house: that stack is the price of keeping the fallback. <!-- claims: extra_vs15_total_now -->
S07.2 It exists because the 30-year carries a higher rate on the same balance, this week 0.67 point higher. <!-- claims: spread_now -->

## S08 — Why paying in 15 matters at all

S08.1 Paid on its own 30-year schedule, that loan would charge $477,622 in interest. <!-- claims: interest_30full_now -->
S08.2 Paid in 15 years, it charges $210,691, so the real comparison is the 15-year loan against the 30-year paid in 15. <!-- claims: interest_30on15_now; hold: 0.8 -->

## S09 — The shortcut (viewer question 2)

S09.1 There's a common shortcut: pay the 30-year loan exactly what the 15-year would cost, and assume it ends on the same day. <!-- claims: pay15_now, pay30on15_now -->
S09.2 At this week's rates, it doesn't: it ends after about 195 months, about 15 months late. <!-- claims: months_at_pay15_now, months_late_at_pay15_now; hold: 1.0 -->
S09.3 To finish in 15 years, she'd add $733 a month on top of the required payment. <!-- claims: extra_principal_needed_now -->
S09.4 And that extra never lowers what the loan requires: the required payment stays where it was, and the loan simply ends sooner. <!-- claims: — -->
S09.5 That's why the fallback is still there in year 10, if a month goes wrong. <!-- claims: — -->

## S10 — Real loans, real weeks

S10.1 Many walk-throughs of this question use one assumed rate and treat paying early as the obvious win. <!-- claims: — -->
S10.2 Here, a real 15-year loan stands next to the 30-year paid in 15, at the real rates of every week since 1991. <!-- claims: first_week, pay30on15_now -->
S10.3 So is Tessa's stack a normal price for that fallback, or is this week unusual? <!-- claims: extra_vs15_total_now; hold: 1.5 -->

>>> MID-ROLL 1 (in the 1.5 s hold after S10.3; end of act 1, act-2 question open)

=== ACT 2 — JOURNEY: the fallback's price in every week since 1991 ===

## S11 — Method

S11.1 We priced the same $320,000 both ways in each of 1,833 weeks, at that week's own survey rates; how it was built is on screen and in the description. <!-- claims: n_weeks, interest_15_now -->
S11.2 Tessa's week is the last of them. <!-- claims: last_week -->

## S12 — The gap is not fixed

S12.1 The price comes down to one thing: how far the 30-year rate sits above the 15-year. <!-- claims: spread_now -->
S12.2 Since 1991, that gap has run from 0.2 point to 1.0 point. <!-- claims: spread_min, spread_max, first_week; hold: 0.8 -->

## S13 — Typical gap

S13.1 It averaged 0.57 point, and was at least half a point in about 2 in 3 weeks. <!-- claims: spread_mean, share_spread_ge_050 -->
S13.2 Tessa's gap this week sits a little above that average. <!-- claims: spread_now, spread_mean -->

## S14 — The cheapest stack

S14.1 Stand a stack beside every week, and the stacks rise and fall with that gap. <!-- claims: — -->
S14.2 The smallest was $6,097, in December 2008. <!-- claims: extra_total_min, extra_total_min_week; hold: 1.0 -->

## S15 — The tallest stack

S15.1 The tallest was $29,502, in January 2023. <!-- claims: extra_total_max, extra_total_max_week; hold: 1.0 -->

## S16 — Tessa's place

S16.1 The typical week, the median, priced the fallback at $16,631. <!-- claims: extra_total_median -->
S16.2 {peak} [serious] Fewer than 1 in 5 weeks since 1991 put a price this high on it. <!-- claims: share_extra_ge_now, first_week, extra_vs15_total_now; hold: 1.5 -->
S16.3 That makes Tessa's fallback expensive by history, not a mistake: what a lower payment is worth in a bad month is something this replay can't measure. <!-- claims: extra_vs15_total_now -->

## S17 — By decade

S17.1 Line the weeks up by decade, and the pattern is not the one most people expect. <!-- claims: — -->
S17.2 In the 1990s, with the 30-year rate typically near 7.73 percent, the typical fallback cost $15,118. <!-- claims: era1991_median_r30, era1991_median_extra_total -->

## S18 — Lower rates, pricier fallback

S18.1 In the 2010s, rates were far lower, typically near 4.03 percent, yet the fallback cost more: $20,374. <!-- claims: era2010_median_r30, era2010_median_extra_total; hold: 1.0 -->

## S19 — The gap explains it

S19.1 The reason is the gap: in the 2010s and 2020s it typically ran about 0.7 point, against about 0.45 in the 1990s and 2000s. <!-- claims: era2020_median_spread, era2010_median_spread, era2000_median_spread, era1991_median_spread -->
S19.2 A lower rate didn't mean a cheaper fallback; a wider gap meant a pricier one. <!-- claims: — ; hold: 1.0 -->

## S20 — Since 2020

S20.1 Since 2020, the typical week priced it at $21,345, close to Tessa's own stack. <!-- claims: era2020_median_extra_total, extra_vs15_total_now -->
S20.2 That's history, not a forecast: the gap has moved before, and nothing here says where it goes. <!-- claims: — -->

## S21 — Once a year instead of monthly (viewer question 3)

S21.1 Tessa has a practical question too: could she send the extra once a year instead of every month? <!-- claims: — -->
S21.2 At this week's rates, that's $8,792 once a year, the same total as the monthly extra. <!-- claims: yearly_lump, extra_principal_needed_now -->
S21.3 Paid that way, the loan ends four months later. <!-- claims: yearly_lump_months; hold: 0.8 -->

## S22 — What the timing costs

S22.1 And it charges about $8,200 more in interest, because each dollar sits on the balance longer before it arrives. <!-- claims: yearly_vs_monthly_interest; hold: 1.0 -->
S22.2 Monthly or yearly is a cash-flow choice; the replay only prices the timing. <!-- claims: — -->
S22.3 Which leaves the question underneath all of this: when Tessa puts an extra dollar into the mortgage, what does it actually earn? <!-- claims: —; hold: 1.5 -->

>>> MID-ROLL 2 (in the 1.5 s hold after S22.3; end of act 2, act-3 question open)

=== ACT 3 — ANSWER: the bar, and Leo ===

## S23 — The bar (viewer question 1)

S23.1 Every extra dollar of principal stops interest from being charged on that dollar, at the loan's own rate. <!-- claims: bar_now -->
S23.2 On Tessa's 30-year, that's 7.40 percent a year, before taxes. <!-- claims: bar_now; hold: 1.0 -->
S23.3 It isn't an investment return; it's interest she no longer pays. <!-- claims: bar_now -->
S23.4 Think of it as a bar: any other use of that dollar has to clear it to come out ahead. <!-- claims: bar_now -->

## S24 — The bar's history

S24.1 The bar moves with the rate a loan was taken at. <!-- claims: — -->
S24.2 Since 1991, it has stood as high as 9.25 percent, in November 1994. <!-- claims: r30_max, r30_max_week, first_week -->

## S25 — The low point

S25.1 And as low as 2.65 percent, in January 2021. <!-- claims: r30_min, r30_min_week; hold: 1.0 -->

## S26 — How high Tessa's bar is

S26.1 Only about 1 week in 5 had a bar as high as Tessa's. <!-- claims: share_r30_ge_now, bar_now; hold: 1.0 -->

## S27 — Leo

S27.1 Leo, also illustrative, took a 30-year loan of the same size in that January 2021 week, at 2.65 percent, and paid it like a 15-year too. <!-- claims: leo_r30, leo_r15, r30_min_week -->
S27.2 His fallback was cheaper: $13,231 over 15 years, about $74 a month. <!-- claims: leo_extra_vs15_total, leo_extra_vs15_month -->

## S28 — Leo's bar

S28.1 And it was bigger: his required payment sat about $793 a month below the 15-year's. <!-- claims: leo_fallback_gap -->
S28.2 But his bar was 2.65 percent: each extra dollar he paid earned only that, before taxes. <!-- claims: leo_r30 -->
S28.3 [thoughtful] Same plan, a different week, and it means something else. <!-- claims: —; hold: 1.0 -->
S28.4 For Leo, the stack was short and the bar was low; for Tessa, the stack is tall and the bar is high. <!-- claims: leo_extra_vs15_total, extra_vs15_total_now -->

## S29 — The threshold

S29.1 For any fixed-rate loan, the bar is that loan's own rate, printed on the paperwork. <!-- claims: bar_now -->
S29.2 And the stack depends on how far apart the 15-year and 30-year offers sit that week. <!-- claims: extra_vs15_total_now, spread_now -->
S29.3 Clearing the bar isn't the whole story: a dollar paid into the house is hard to get back in a bad month, which is exactly what the fallback is for. <!-- claims: —; hold: 1.0 -->

=== LIMITS ===

## S30 — Limits and method

S30.1 How this was built is on the method card and in the description. <!-- claims: — -->
S30.2 The rates are weekly US survey averages for borrowers with strong credit and a large down payment; real offers differ in points, fees and terms. <!-- claims: — -->
S30.3 Payments here are principal and interest only: no property taxes, no homeowners insurance, no private mortgage insurance, no tax deductions. <!-- claims: — -->
S30.4 The bar is before taxes, and it isn't compared with any market return here. <!-- claims: bar_now -->
S30.5 What a lower payment is worth in a job loss or an emergency isn't measured. <!-- claims: — -->
S30.6 Tessa's numbers hold only at this week's rates on $320,000; another offer gives another stack. <!-- claims: extra_vs15_total_now, interest_15_now -->
S30.7 This is US only, and it's history, not a forecast; it doesn't say which loan to take. <!-- claims: —; hold: 1.0 -->

## S31 — Tessa's answer

S31.1 Tessa asked: a 15-year, or a 30-year paid in 15? <!-- claims: pay30on15_now -->
S31.2 [thoughtful] Her answer: the 30-year paid in 15 is the 15-year plus a fallback, and this week, that fallback costs her $120 a month. <!-- claims: extra_vs15_month_now, pay30on15_now; hold: 1.5 -->

+print(f'\n{len(rows)} câu, {len(alltext.split())} từ viết ({SPOKEN} từ đọc), độ dài ước {fmt(EST)} ({SPOKEN} / {WPS_TOTAL} từ/s, {FORMAT}); '
+      f'trục mốc giây {fmt(TOTAL)} ({WPS_SPEECH} từ/s + hold {sum(r["hold"] for r in rows):.1f} s + ident {IDENT_S:.0f} s)')
+print(f'| Phần | Từ | Thời gian | Tỉ lệ | Khuôn {FORMAT} | Δ |')
+for p in order:
+    s, e = bounds[p]
+    share = (e - s) / TOTAL * 100
+    wc = sum(len(r['text'].split()) for r in rows if r['part'] == p)

+    print(f'| {p} | {wc} | {fmt(s)}–{fmt(e)} | {share:.1f} % | {TEMPLATE.get(p, "—")} % | {d:+.1f}{"  ← > ±5 (THAM KHẢO, nêu ở C2)" if abs(d) > 5 else ""} |')
+    if abs(d) > 5:
+        warn.append(f'khuôn tỉ lệ: {p} lệch {d:+.1f} điểm')
+NMID = {'101': (1, 1), 'lab': (2, 2), 'deep': (2, 3)}.get(FORMAT, (1, 1))   # (ít nhất, nhiều nhất)
+# T6-1: dòng "mid-roll đủ điều kiện hay không" cho gói G1; tập < 8:00 không được ghi là có mid-roll
+_mr_ok = EST >= MIDROLL_MIN_S
+print(f'mid-roll: {"ĐỦ" if _mr_ok else "KHÔNG ĐỦ"} điều kiện theo độ dài ước {fmt(EST)} (cần ≥ 8:00 thật; ≥ 2 phút đầu/cuối; lặng ≥ 1 s) — '
+      'chốt bằng độ dài thật sau khi sinh lời (≥ 8:10) và ở C5 (≥ 8:00)')
+if mid and not _mr_ok:
+    warn.append(f'mid-roll khai trong kịch bản nhưng độ dài ước {fmt(EST)} < 8:00 — không được ghi là có mid-roll (T6-1)')
+if FORMAT == 'deep':   # episode.md §9: 2 điểm khi < 15:30, 3 khi ≥ 15:30 (theo độ dài ước; chốt lại trên độ dài thật)
+    NMID = (3, 3) if EST >= 930 else (2, 2)

+    fail.append(f'mid-roll: {len(mid)} điểm ({FORMAT} cần {NMID[0]}–{NMID[1]}; bỏ mid-roll chỉ khi G1 duyệt, --g1-short)')

+else:

+

+if os.path.exists(HOOKS):

+        m = re.match(r'^(H[ABC])\.(\d+)\s+\{(\w+)\}\s+((?:\[[a-z ]+\]\s+)?)(.*?)\s*<!--\s*claims:\s*(.*?)\s*-->\s*$', ln.rstrip('\n'))
+        if m:

# Script — Episode 7 (format `lab`, C2 v1, WRITER, 2026-10-11)

(header filled after the checker run)

---

=== COLD OPEN ===

## S01 — Tessa's fallback has a price

S01.1 {hook} Tessa's mortgage fallback costs $120 a month. <!-- claims: extra_vs15_month_now -->
S01.2 {hook} She's borrowing $320,000 this week, and in her city that payment is already her biggest bill. <!-- claims: interest_15_now, last_week -->

## S02 — Her question, and the promise

S02.1 {question} [curious] A 15-year mortgage, or a 30-year she pays off in 15 years anyway, with its lower payment kept for a bad month? <!-- claims: pay30on15_now -->
S02.2 {promise} We replayed every week the US survey priced both loans, to put that fallback in dollars, and to find what each extra dollar of principal earns. <!-- claims: n_weeks; hold: 0.5 -->

## S03 — Who Tessa is, this week's rates, the limits (shared continuation for all three hooks)

S03.1 {hook} Tessa is illustrative, but her rates are real: this week's survey has the 15-year at 6.73 percent and the 30-year at 7.40. <!-- claims: r15_now, r30_now -->
S03.2 {constraint} This is US only, and it's history, not a forecast. <!-- claims: — -->
S03.3 {constraint} It won't say which loan to take, or whether to invest. <!-- claims: —; hold: 0.8 -->

=== IDENT (3 s, no narration) ===

=== ACT 1 — CONTEXT: two loans, one fallback, and what it costs Tessa ===

## S04 — Two payments

S04.1 {hook} Here is what Tessa is weighing. <!-- claims: — -->
S04.2 {hook} On $320,000, the 15-year loan's payment is $2,828 a month. <!-- claims: pay15_now, interest_15_now -->
S04.3 {hook} The 30-year loan only requires $2,216. <!-- claims: pay30_now; hold: 0.8 -->

## S05 — The fallback

S05.1 That gap, about $613 a month, is the fallback: in a tight month, it's the least the 30-year asks of her. <!-- claims: fallback_gap_now; hold: 1.0 -->
S05.2 The bigger payment fits her budget today, but only just, and a job change or a big repair could squeeze it. <!-- claims: — -->
S05.3 Still, she wants the house paid off in 15 years, so the 30-year only works for her if she pays it like a short loan. <!-- claims: pay30on15_now -->

## S06 — The price of paying the 30-year in 15

S06.1 At 7.40 percent, finishing that loan in 15 years takes $2,948 a month. <!-- claims: pay30on15_now, r30_now -->
S06.2 That's $120 a month more than the 15-year loan, for the same house and the same 15 years. <!-- claims: extra_vs15_month_now, pay30on15_now -->
S06.3 Over those 15 years, the extra adds up to $21,622. <!-- claims: extra_vs15_total_now; hold: 1.2 -->

## S07 — The stack

S07.1 In Tessa's world, that price is a stack of bills beside her house: the stack is what keeping the fallback costs. <!-- claims: extra_vs15_total_now -->
S07.2 It exists because the 30-year carries a higher rate on the same balance, this week 0.67 point higher. <!-- claims: spread_now -->

## S08 — Why paying in 15 matters at all

S08.1 Paid on its own 30-year schedule, her loan would charge $477,622 in interest. <!-- claims: interest_30full_now -->
S08.2 Paid in 15 years, it charges $210,691. <!-- claims: interest_30on15_now; hold: 0.8 -->

## S09 — The stack, as a difference

S09.1 The 15-year loan charges $189,069, and the difference between those last two totals is exactly the stack. <!-- claims: interest_15_now, interest_30on15_now, extra_vs15_total_now; hold: 0.8 -->
S09.2 So the 30-year paid in 15 isn't the same loan as the 15-year: it's the 15-year plus a fallback, and the fallback has a price. <!-- claims: pay30on15_now, extra_vs15_total_now -->
S09.3 Is Tessa's stack a normal price for that fallback, or is this week unusual? <!-- claims: extra_vs15_total_now; hold: 1.5 -->

>>> MID-ROLL 1 (in the 1.5 s hold after S09.3; end of act 1, act-2 question open)

=== ACT 2 — JOURNEY: the fallback's price in every week since 1991, and Tessa's plan tested ===

## S10 — Real loans, real weeks, and the method

S10.1 Many walk-throughs of this question use one assumed rate and treat paying early as the obvious win. <!-- claims: — -->
S10.2 Here, a real 15-year loan stands next to the 30-year paid in 15, at the real rates of every week since 1991. <!-- claims: first_week, pay30on15_now -->
S10.3 We priced the same $320,000 both ways in each of 1,833 weeks, at that week's own survey rates; how it was built is on screen and in the description. <!-- claims: n_weeks, interest_15_now -->
S10.4 Tessa's week is the last of them, and in every earlier week we asked her question: what would the fallback have cost then? <!-- claims: last_week -->

## S11 — The gap is not fixed

S11.1 The answer comes down to one thing: how far the 30-year rate sits above the 15-year. <!-- claims: spread_now -->
S11.2 Since 1991, that gap has run from 0.2 point to 1.0 point. <!-- claims: spread_min, spread_max, first_week; hold: 0.8 -->

## S12 — Typical gap

S12.1 It averaged 0.57 point, and was at least half a point in about 2 in 3 weeks. <!-- claims: spread_mean, share_spread_ge_050 -->
S12.2 Tessa's gap this week sits a little above that average. <!-- claims: spread_now, spread_mean -->

## S13 — The smallest stack

S13.1 Stand a stack beside every week, and the stacks rise and fall with that gap. <!-- claims: — -->
S13.2 The smallest was $6,097, in December 2008. <!-- claims: extra_total_min, extra_total_min_week; hold: 1.0 -->

## S14 — The tallest stack

S14.1 The tallest was $29,502, in January 2023. <!-- claims: extra_total_max, extra_total_max_week; hold: 1.0 -->

## S15 — Tessa's place

S15.1 The typical week, the median, priced the fallback at $16,631. <!-- claims: extra_total_median -->
S15.2 {peak} [serious] Fewer than 1 in 5 weeks since 1991 put a price this high on it. <!-- claims: share_extra_ge_now, first_week, extra_vs15_total_now; hold: 1.5 -->
S15.3 That makes Tessa's fallback expensive by history, not a mistake: what a lower payment is worth in a bad month is something this replay can't measure. <!-- claims: extra_vs15_total_now -->

## S16 — By decade: the 1990s

S16.1 Line the weeks up by decade, and the pattern is not the one most people expect. <!-- claims: — -->
S16.2 In the 1990s, with the 30-year rate typically near 7.73 percent, the typical fallback cost $15,118. <!-- claims: era1991_median_r30, era1991_median_extra_total -->

## S17 — The 2000s

S17.1 In the 2000s, with rates near 6.18 percent, it cost about the same: $14,210. <!-- claims: era2000_median_r30, era2000_median_extra_total -->

## S18 — Lower rates, pricier fallback

S18.1 In the 2010s, rates were far lower, typically near 4.03 percent, yet the fallback cost more: $20,374. <!-- claims: era2010_median_r30, era2010_median_extra_total; hold: 1.0 -->

## S19 — The gap explains it

S19.1 The reason is the gap: in the 2010s and 2020s it typically ran about 0.7 point, against about 0.45 in the 1990s and 2000s. <!-- claims: era2020_median_spread, era2010_median_spread, era2000_median_spread, era1991_median_spread -->
S19.2 A lower rate didn't mean a cheaper fallback; a wider gap meant a pricier one. <!-- claims: —; hold: 1.0 -->

## S20 — Since 2020

S20.1 Since 2020, the typical week priced it at $21,345, close to Tessa's own stack. <!-- claims: era2020_median_extra_total, extra_vs15_total_now -->
S20.2 That's history, not a forecast: the gap has moved before, and nothing here says where it goes. <!-- claims: — -->

## S21 — The shortcut (viewer question 2)

S21.1 Back to Tessa's own loan, and a shortcut many people reach for: pay the 30-year exactly what the 15-year would cost, and assume it ends on the same day. <!-- claims: pay15_now, pay30on15_now -->
S21.2 At this week's rates, it doesn't: it ends after about 195 months, about 15 months late. <!-- claims: months_at_pay15_now, months_late_at_pay15_now; hold: 1.0 -->
S21.3 To finish in 15 years, she'd add $733 a month on top of the required payment. <!-- claims: extra_principal_needed_now -->

## S22 — The extra doesn't touch the required payment

S22.1 That extra never lowers what the loan requires: the required payment stays where it was, and the loan simply ends sooner. <!-- claims: — -->
S22.2 That's why the fallback is still there years later, if a month goes wrong. <!-- claims: — -->

## S23 — Once a year instead of monthly (viewer question 3)

S23.1 Tessa has another practical question: could she send the extra once a year instead of every month? <!-- claims: — -->
S23.2 At this week's rates, that's $8,792 once a year, the same total as the monthly extra. <!-- claims: yearly_lump, extra_principal_needed_now -->
S23.3 Paid that way, the loan ends four months later. <!-- claims: yearly_lump_months; hold: 0.8 -->

## S24 — What the timing costs

S24.1 And it charges about $8,200 more in interest, because each dollar sits on the balance longer before it arrives. <!-- claims: yearly_vs_monthly_interest; hold: 1.0 -->
S24.2 Monthly or yearly is a cash-flow choice; the replay only prices the timing. <!-- claims: — -->
S24.3 Which leaves the question underneath all of this: when Tessa puts an extra dollar into the mortgage, what does it actually earn? <!-- claims: —; hold: 1.5 -->

>>> MID-ROLL 2 (in the 1.5 s hold after S24.3; end of act 2, act-3 question open)


=== ACT 3 — ANSWER: the bar, and Leo ===

## S23 — The bar (viewer question 1)

S23.1 Every extra dollar of principal stops interest from being charged on that dollar, at the loan's own rate. <!-- claims: bar_now -->
S23.2 On Tessa's 30-year, that's 7.40 percent a year, before taxes. <!-- claims: bar_now; hold: 1.0 -->
S23.3 It isn't an investment return; it's interest she no longer pays. <!-- claims: bar_now -->
S23.4 Think of it as a bar: any other use of that dollar has to clear it to come out ahead. <!-- claims: bar_now -->

## S24 — The bar's history

S24.1 The bar moves with the rate a loan was taken at. <!-- claims: — -->
S24.2 Since 1991, it has stood as high as 9.25 percent, in November 1994. <!-- claims: r30_max, r30_max_week, first_week -->

## S25 — The low point

S25.1 And as low as 2.65 percent, in January 2021. <!-- claims: r30_min, r30_min_week; hold: 1.0 -->

## S26 — How high Tessa's bar is

S26.1 Only about 1 week in 5 had a bar as high as Tessa's. <!-- claims: share_r30_ge_now, bar_now; hold: 1.0 -->

## S27 — Leo

S27.1 Leo, also illustrative, took a 30-year loan of the same size in that January 2021 week, at 2.65 percent, and paid it like a 15-year too. <!-- claims: leo_r30, leo_r15, r30_min_week -->
S27.2 His fallback was cheaper: $13,231 over 15 years, about $74 a month. <!-- claims: leo_extra_vs15_total, leo_extra_vs15_month -->

## S28 — Leo's bar

S28.1 And it was bigger: his required payment sat about $793 a month below the 15-year's. <!-- claims: leo_fallback_gap -->
S28.2 But his bar was 2.65 percent: each extra dollar he paid earned only that, before taxes. <!-- claims: leo_r30 -->
S28.3 [thoughtful] Same plan, a different week, and it means something else. <!-- claims: —; hold: 1.0 -->
S28.4 For Leo, the stack was short and the bar was low; for Tessa, the stack is tall and the bar is high. <!-- claims: leo_extra_vs15_total, extra_vs15_total_now -->

## S29 — The threshold

S29.1 For any fixed-rate loan, the bar is that loan's own rate, printed on the paperwork. <!-- claims: bar_now -->
S29.2 And the stack depends on how far apart the 15-year and 30-year offers sit that week. <!-- claims: extra_vs15_total_now, spread_now -->
S29.3 Clearing the bar isn't the whole story: a dollar paid into the house is hard to get back in a bad month, which is exactly what the fallback is for. <!-- claims: —; hold: 1.0 -->

=== LIMITS ===

## S30 — Limits and method

S30.1 How this was built is on the method card and in the description. <!-- claims: — -->
S30.2 The rates are weekly US survey averages for borrowers with strong credit and a large down payment; real offers differ in points, fees and terms. <!-- claims: — -->
S30.3 Payments here are principal and interest only: no property taxes, no homeowners insurance, no private mortgage insurance, no tax deductions. <!-- claims: — -->
S30.4 The bar is before taxes, and it isn't compared with any market return here. <!-- claims: bar_now -->
S30.5 What a lower payment is worth in a job loss or an emergency isn't measured. <!-- claims: — -->
S30.6 Tessa's numbers hold only at this week's rates on $320,000; another offer gives another stack. <!-- claims: extra_vs15_total_now, interest_15_now -->
S30.7 This is US only, and it's history, not a forecast; it doesn't say which loan to take. <!-- claims: —; hold: 1.0 -->

## S31 — Tessa's answer

S31.1 Tessa asked: a 15-year, or a 30-year paid in 15? <!-- claims: pay30on15_now -->
S31.2 [thoughtful] Her answer: the 30-year paid in 15 is the 15-year plus a fallback, and this week, that fallback costs her $120 a month. <!-- claims: extra_vs15_month_now, pay30on15_now; hold: 1.5 -->

+
+S20.1 Since 2020, the typical week priced it at $21,345, close to Tessa's own stack. <!-- claims: era2020_median_extra_total, extra_vs15_total_now -->
+S20.2 That's history, not a forecast: the gap has moved before, and nothing here says where it goes. <!-- claims: — -->
+
+## S21 — The shortcut (viewer question 2)
+
+S21.1 Back to Tessa's own loan, and a shortcut many people reach for: pay the 30-year exactly what the 15-year would cost, and assume it ends on the same day. <!-- claims: pay15_now, pay30on15_now -->
+S21.2 At this week's rates, it doesn't: it ends after about 195 months, about 15 months late. <!-- claims: months_at_pay15_now, months_late_at_pay15_now; hold: 1.0 -->
+S21.3 To finish in 15 years, she'd add $733 a month on top of the required payment. <!-- claims: extra_principal_needed_now -->
+
+## S22 — The extra doesn't touch the required payment
+
+S22.1 That extra never lowers what the loan requires: the required payment stays where it was, and the loan simply ends sooner. <!-- claims: — -->
+S22.2 That's why the fallback is still there years later, if a month goes wrong. <!-- claims: — -->

+

# Beats — Episode 7 (format `lab`, C2 v1, WRITER, 2026-10-11)

Times from `check_script.py` (2.66 spoken words/s with numbers read out, scripted holds, 3 s ident; timeline axis 10:06); runtime est. **10:37** at 2.40 words/s for the whole episode (1,528 spoken words). Scene ids = `script.md`. Hook used: **H-B "Chi phí ẩn"** (`hooks.md`).
**Type 1** = the picture carries the meaning on its own ("muted read" = what a muted viewer must read off the picture). **Type 2** = the picture illustrates the narration.

**CENTRAL OBJECT: "the stack"** — W2 `Stack` (fixed bundle denomination), a stack of bills standing beside Tessa's house = the dollar price of the fallback over 15 years (`extra_vs15_total_now`, $21,622 this week). Named "the stack" in narration from S07.1 to S33.1 and labelled "the stack" on screen. **Second object: "the bar"** — W3 `Beam` at the height of the loan's rate = what each extra dollar of principal earns, before taxes (`bar_now`), from S25.4. Thumbnail idea for G1: the stack beside a low-poly house + text "$21,622" / "15 or 30?" (number = claim; Tessa's house carries the ILLUSTRATIVE badge).

**Five character rules (story §2b, episode.md §3.10) — stated and obeyed:**
1. **Lead character: Tessa** (ILLUSTRATIVE; built from dossier situation 2: a buyer in a high-cost metro with a large payment and a tight budget, wondering whether a 15-year payoff is realistic). Borrows $320,000 in the week of October 8, 2026. First sentence (S01.1, 0:00), named as illustrative at S03.1 (≈ 0:30).
2. **She walks through the method:** S10.4 "Tessa's week is the last of them, and in every earlier week we asked her question"; S12.2 her gap against the average; S15.2–S15.3 her place among 1,833 weeks; S20.1 "close to Tessa's own stack"; S21–S23 her own plan tested (viewer questions 2 and 3).
3. **No character promise** in the cold open (`promise_character` not used, M6 = 0); Leo is not announced, he appears in act 3 (S29.1).
4. **Peak line** S15.2 `{peak}` [serious]: *"Fewer than 1 in 5 weeks since 1991 put a price this high on it."* — **14 words, one idea.**
5. **Last sentence is hers and answers her cold-open question** (S02.1 "A 15-year mortgage, or a 30-year paid off in 15 years anyway…?"): S33.3 *"Her answer: the 30-year paid in 15 is the 15-year plus a fallback, and this week, that fallback costs her $120 a month."*
6. **Concrete object:** the stack (bundles of fixed size) and the bar; every height maps to a claim.
Counterweight (act 3, ILLUSTRATIVE): **Leo** — 30-year at 2.65 % in the week of January 7, 2021 (`leo_*`, = `r30_min_week`): smaller stack ($13,231), bigger fallback (about $793), low bar (2.65 %).

**Viewer questions answered (dossier `market/topics/q13-15-vs-30-mortgage.md`, 4 of 5):**
- **Q1** (prepay or invest?) → **S25** (each extra dollar earns the loan's rate = the bar every other use has to clear, before taxes; not an investment return; no market return compared), S26–S28 (the bar's history), S30 (Leo's low bar), S31.3 (liquidity counterweight).
- **Q2** (how much faster with extra principal; how much more for a target date) → **S21** (paying the 15-year amount on the 30-year: about 195 months, about 15 months late; $733 a month on top to finish in 15 years).
- **Q3** (yearly lump vs monthly) → **S23–S24** ($8,792 once a year: four months later, about $8,200 more interest).
- **Q5** (why extra principal doesn't lower the payment) → **S22** (no new number: the required payment stays put, the loan ends sooner, so the fallback survives).
- Q4 (PMI removal) not answered; PMI named only as excluded (S32.3).
**Competitor weakness (one beat, no channel named):** S10.1–S10.2 ("one assumed rate … paying early as the obvious win" → a real 15-year loan beside the 30-year paid in 15, at every week's real rates). **Anchor gap** ("doesn't price an actual 15-year loan alongside it"; "no real rate history"): S10.2 + S10.3, B10.

**New symbols for C3: 1 (+ 1 adapted).**
- **N1 · Month track** (D-010 world, new `lib3d` object): a straight row of 180 identical low-poly tiles running from Tessa's house, one tile per monthly payment; tiles past 180 are `warn`. Shows payoff dates: 15 extra `warn` tiles for "about 15 months late" (S21), 4 for the yearly lump (S23). **Reason it is new:** the library has no object for a count of months / a payoff date; W2 `Stack` means dollars and W5 `Ribbon` means a value over time. **New symbol → C3.**
- **V4 adapted** (S04, S09): "one person, two offers" — the library V4 means fixed vs floating with a fixed line through both cards; here both cards are fixed-rate (15-year / 30-year paid in 15) and the line through both is the $2,828 → $2,948 level. Re-check at C3 (same check as a new symbol).
- Everything else is library: W1 `House`, W2 `Stack`, W3 `Beam` (the bar), W4 `Person` (faceless, ILLUSTRATIVE), W5 `Ribbon` (stack tops through 1,833 weeks), V1 (replay grid, 1,833 cells), V3 (rate line against a fixed line), V6 (gap bracket, always labelled; type 2), V7 (method card), meaning labels.

# Script — Episode 7 (format `lab`, C2 v1, WRITER, 2026-10-11)

(header filled after the checker run)

---

=== COLD OPEN ===

## S01 — Tessa's fallback has a price

S01.1 {hook} Tessa's mortgage fallback costs $120 a month. <!-- claims: extra_vs15_month_now -->
S01.2 {hook} She's borrowing $320,000 this week, and in her city that payment is her biggest bill. <!-- claims: interest_15_now, last_week -->

## S02 — Her question, and the promise

S02.1 {question} [curious] A 15-year mortgage, or a 30-year paid off in 15 years anyway, with its lower payment kept for a bad month? <!-- claims: pay30on15_now -->
S02.2 {promise} We replayed every week the US survey priced both loans, to put that fallback in dollars and find what each extra dollar of principal earns. <!-- claims: n_weeks; hold: 0.5 -->

## S03 — Who Tessa is, this week's rates, the limits (shared continuation for all three hooks)

S03.1 {hook} Tessa is illustrative, but her rates are real: this week's survey has the 15-year at 6.73 percent and the 30-year at 7.40. <!-- claims: r15_now, r30_now -->
S03.2 {constraint} This is US only, and it's history, not a forecast. <!-- claims: — -->
S03.3 {constraint} It won't say which loan to take, or whether to invest. <!-- claims: —; hold: 0.8 -->

=== IDENT (3 s, no narration) ===

=== ACT 1 — CONTEXT: two loans, one fallback, and what it costs Tessa ===

## S04 — Two payments

S04.1 {hook} Here is what Tessa is weighing. <!-- claims: — -->
S04.2 {hook} On $320,000, the 15-year loan's payment is $2,828 a month. <!-- claims: pay15_now, interest_15_now -->
S04.3 {hook} The 30-year loan only requires $2,216. <!-- claims: pay30_now; hold: 0.8 -->

## S05 — The fallback

S05.1 That gap, about $613 a month, is the fallback: in a tight month, it's the least the 30-year asks of her. <!-- claims: fallback_gap_now; hold: 1.0 -->
S05.2 The bigger payment fits her budget today, but only just, and a job change or a big repair could squeeze it. <!-- claims: — -->
S05.3 Still, she wants the house paid off in 15 years, so the 30-year only works for her if she pays it like a short loan. <!-- claims: pay30on15_now -->

## S06 — The price of paying the 30-year in 15

S06.1 At 7.40 percent, finishing that loan in 15 years takes $2,948 a month. <!-- claims: pay30on15_now, r30_now -->
S06.2 That's $120 a month more than the 15-year loan, for the same house and the same 15 years. <!-- claims: extra_vs15_month_now, pay30on15_now -->
S06.3 Over those 15 years, the extra adds up to $21,622. <!-- claims: extra_vs15_total_now; hold: 1.2 -->

## S07 — The stack

S07.1 In Tessa's world, that price is a stack of bills beside her house: the stack is what keeping the fallback costs. <!-- claims: extra_vs15_total_now -->
S07.2 It exists because the 30-year carries a higher rate on the same balance, this week 0.67 point higher. <!-- claims: spread_now -->

## S08 — Why paying in 15 matters at all

S08.1 Paid on its own 30-year schedule, her loan would charge $477,622 in interest. <!-- claims: interest_30full_now; hold: 1.0 -->
S08.2 Paid in 15 years, it charges $210,691. <!-- claims: interest_30on15_now; hold: 0.8 -->

## S09 — The stack, as a difference

S09.1 The 15-year loan charges $189,069, and the difference between those last two totals is exactly the stack. <!-- claims: interest_15_now, interest_30on15_now, extra_vs15_total_now; hold: 0.8 -->
S09.2 So the 30-year paid in 15 isn't the same loan as the 15-year: it's the 15-year plus a fallback, and the fallback has a price. <!-- claims: pay30on15_now, extra_vs15_total_now -->
S09.3 Is Tessa's stack a normal price for that fallback, or is this week unusual? <!-- claims: extra_vs15_total_now; hold: 1.5 -->

>>> MID-ROLL 1 (in the 1.5 s hold after S09.3; end of act 1, act-2 question open)

=== ACT 2 — JOURNEY: the fallback's price in every week since 1991, and Tessa's plan tested ===

## S10 — Real loans, real weeks, and the method

S10.1 Many walk-throughs of this question use one assumed rate and treat paying early as the obvious win. <!-- claims: — -->
S10.2 Here, a real 15-year loan stands next to the 30-year paid in 15, at the real rates of every week since 1991. <!-- claims: first_week, pay30on15_now; hold: 0.8 -->
S10.3 We priced the same $320,000 both ways in each of 1,833 weeks, at that week's own survey rates; how it was built is on screen and in the description. <!-- claims: n_weeks, interest_15_now -->
S10.4 Tessa's week is the last of them, and in every earlier week we asked her question: what would the fallback have cost then? <!-- claims: last_week -->

## S11 — The gap is not fixed

S11.1 The answer comes down to one thing: how far the 30-year rate sits above the 15-year. <!-- claims: spread_now -->
S11.2 Since 1991, that gap has run from 0.2 point to 1.0 point. <!-- claims: spread_min, spread_max, first_week; hold: 1.2 -->

## S12 — Typical gap

S12.1 It averaged 0.57 point, and was at least half a point in about 2 in 3 weeks. <!-- claims: spread_mean, share_spread_ge_050 -->
S12.2 Tessa's gap this week sits a little above that average. <!-- claims: spread_now, spread_mean -->

## S13 — The smallest stack

S13.1 Stand a stack beside every week, and the stacks rise and fall with that gap. <!-- claims: — -->
S13.2 The smallest was $6,097, in December 2008. <!-- claims: extra_total_min, extra_total_min_week; hold: 1.0 -->

## S14 — The tallest stack

S14.1 The tallest was $29,502, in January 2023. <!-- claims: extra_total_max, extra_total_max_week; hold: 1.0 -->

## S15 — Tessa's place

S15.1 The typical week, the median, priced the fallback at $16,631. <!-- claims: extra_total_median -->
S15.2 {peak} [serious] Fewer than 1 in 5 weeks since 1991 put a price this high on it. <!-- claims: share_extra_ge_now, first_week, extra_vs15_total_now; hold: 1.5 -->
S15.3 That makes Tessa's fallback expensive by history, not a mistake: what a lower payment is worth in a bad month is something this replay can't measure. <!-- claims: extra_vs15_total_now -->

## S16 — By decade: the 1990s

S16.1 Line the weeks up by decade, and the pattern is not the one most people expect. <!-- claims: — -->
S16.2 In the 1990s, with the 30-year rate typically near 7.73 percent, the typical fallback cost $15,118. <!-- claims: era1991_median_r30, era1991_median_extra_total -->

## S17 — The 2000s

S17.1 In the 2000s, with rates near 6.18 percent, it cost about the same: $14,210. <!-- claims: era2000_median_r30, era2000_median_extra_total -->

## S18 — Lower rates, pricier fallback

S18.1 In the 2010s, rates were far lower, typically near 4.03 percent, yet the fallback cost more: $20,374. <!-- claims: era2010_median_r30, era2010_median_extra_total; hold: 1.0 -->

## S19 — The gap explains it

S19.1 The reason is the gap: in the 2010s and 2020s it typically ran about 0.7 point, against about 0.45 in the 1990s and 2000s. <!-- claims: era2020_median_spread, era2010_median_spread, era2000_median_spread, era1991_median_spread -->
S19.2 A lower rate didn't mean a cheaper fallback; a wider gap meant a pricier one. <!-- claims: —; hold: 1.0 -->

## S20 — Since 2020

S20.1 Since 2020, the typical week priced it at $21,345, close to Tessa's own stack. <!-- claims: era2020_median_extra_total, extra_vs15_total_now -->
S20.2 That's history, not a forecast: the gap has moved before, and nothing here says where it goes. <!-- claims: — -->

## S21 — The shortcut (viewer question 2)

S21.1 Back to Tessa's own loan, and a shortcut many people reach for: pay the 30-year exactly what the 15-year would cost, and assume it ends on the same day. <!-- claims: pay15_now, pay30on15_now -->
S21.2 At this week's rates, it doesn't: it ends after about 195 months, about 15 months late. <!-- claims: months_at_pay15_now, months_late_at_pay15_now; hold: 1.0 -->
S21.3 To finish in 15 years, she'd add $733 a month on top of the required payment. <!-- claims: extra_principal_needed_now -->

## S22 — The extra doesn't touch the required payment

S22.1 That extra never lowers what the loan requires: the required payment stays where it was, and the loan simply ends sooner. <!-- claims: — -->
S22.2 That's why the fallback is still there years later, if a month goes wrong. <!-- claims: — -->

## S23 — Once a year instead of monthly (viewer question 3)

S23.1 Tessa has another practical question: could she send the extra once a year instead of every month? <!-- claims: — -->
S23.2 At this week's rates, that's $8,792 once a year, the same total as the monthly extra. <!-- claims: yearly_lump, extra_principal_needed_now -->
S23.3 Paid that way, the loan ends four months later. <!-- claims: yearly_lump_months; hold: 0.8 -->

## S24 — What the timing costs

S24.1 And it charges about $8,200 more in interest, because each dollar sits on the balance longer before it arrives. <!-- claims: yearly_vs_monthly_interest; hold: 1.0 -->
S24.2 Monthly or yearly is a cash-flow choice; the replay only prices the timing. <!-- claims: — -->
S24.3 Which leaves the question underneath all of this: when Tessa puts an extra dollar into the mortgage, what does it actually earn? <!-- claims: —; hold: 1.5 -->

>>> MID-ROLL 2 (in the 1.5 s hold after S24.3; end of act 2, act-3 question open)


=== ACT 3 — ANSWER: the bar, Leo, and the threshold ===

## S25 — The bar (viewer question 1)

S25.1 Every extra dollar of principal stops interest from being charged on that dollar, at the loan's own rate. <!-- claims: bar_now -->
S25.2 On Tessa's 30-year, that's 7.40 percent a year, before taxes. <!-- claims: bar_now; hold: 1.0 -->
S25.3 It isn't an investment return; it's interest she no longer pays. <!-- claims: bar_now -->
S25.4 That rate is the bar: any other use of that dollar has to clear it to come out ahead. <!-- claims: bar_now -->

## S26 — The bar's history

S26.1 The bar moves with the rate a loan was taken at. <!-- claims: — -->
S26.2 Since 1991, it has stood as high as 9.25 percent, in November 1994. <!-- claims: r30_max, r30_max_week, first_week; hold: 1.0 -->

## S27 — The low point

S27.1 And as low as 2.65 percent, in January 2021. <!-- claims: r30_min, r30_min_week; hold: 1.0 -->

## S28 — How high Tessa's bar is

S28.1 Only about 1 week in 5 had a bar as high as Tessa's. <!-- claims: share_r30_ge_now, bar_now; hold: 1.0 -->

## S29 — Leo

S29.1 Leo, also illustrative, took a 30-year loan of the same size in that January 2021 week, at 2.65 percent, and paid it like a 15-year too. <!-- claims: leo_r30, leo_r15, r30_min_week -->
S29.2 His fallback was cheaper: $13,231 over 15 years, about $74 a month. <!-- claims: leo_extra_vs15_total, leo_extra_vs15_month -->

## S30 — Leo's bar

S30.1 And it was bigger: his required payment sat about $793 a month below the 15-year's. <!-- claims: leo_fallback_gap -->
S30.2 But his bar was 2.65 percent: each extra dollar he paid earned only that, before taxes. <!-- claims: leo_r30 -->
S30.3 [thoughtful] Same plan, a different week, and it means something else. <!-- claims: —; hold: 1.0 -->
S30.4 For Leo, the stack was short and the bar was low; for Tessa, the stack is tall and the bar is high. <!-- claims: leo_extra_vs15_total, extra_vs15_total_now -->

+S09.3 Is Tessa's stack a normal price for that fallback, or is this week unusual? <!-- claims: extra_vs15_total_now; hold: 1.5 -->

+
+S10.1 Many walk-throughs of this question use one assumed rate and treat paying early as the obvious win. <!-- claims: — -->

+S15.3 That makes Tessa's fallback expensive by history, not a mistake: what a lower payment is worth in a bad month is something this replay can't measure. <!-- claims: extra_vs15_total_now -->
+
+## S16 — By decade: the 1990s
+
+S16.1 Line the weeks up by decade, and the pattern is not the one most people expect. <!-- claims: — -->
+S16.2 In the 1990s, with the 30-year rate typically near 7.73 percent, the typical fallback cost $15,118. <!-- claims: era1991_median_r30, era1991_median_extra_total -->

+## S17 — The 2000s
+
+S17.1 In the 2000s, with rates near 6.18 percent, it cost about the same: $14,210. <!-- claims: era2000_median_r30, era2000_median_extra_total -->

+## S18 — Lower rates, pricier fallback
+
+S18.1 In the 2010s, rates were far lower, typically near 4.03 percent, yet the fallback cost more: $20,374. <!-- claims: era2010_median_r30, era2010_median_extra_total; hold: 1.0 -->

+S19.1 The reason is the gap: in the 2010s and 2020s it typically ran about 0.7 point, against about 0.45 in the 1990s and 2000s. <!-- claims: era2020_median_spread, era2010_median_spread, era2000_median_spread, era1991_median_spread -->
+S19.2 A lower rate didn't mean a cheaper fallback; a wider gap meant a pricier one. <!-- claims: —; hold: 1.0 -->

+S21.3 To finish in 15 years, she'd add $733 a month on top of the required payment. <!-- claims: extra_principal_needed_now -->

+
+S22.1 That extra never lowers what the loan requires: the required payment stays where it was, and the loan simply ends sooner. <!-- claims: — -->
+S22.2 That's why the fallback is still there years later, if a month goes wrong. <!-- claims: — -->

+
+S23.1 Tessa has another practical question: could she send the extra once a year instead of every month? <!-- claims: — -->

+
+S24.1 And it charges about $8,200 more in interest, because each dollar sits on the balance longer before it arrives. <!-- claims: yearly_vs_monthly_interest; hold: 1.0 -->
+S24.2 Monthly or yearly is a cash-flow choice; the replay only prices the timing. <!-- claims: — -->

+

+
+S25.1 Every extra dollar of principal stops interest from being charged on that dollar, at the loan's own rate. <!-- claims: bar_now -->

+S25.3 It isn't an investment return; it's interest she no longer pays. <!-- claims: bar_now -->

- **Câu hỏi khán giả (4/5):** Q1 ở S25 (thêm S26–S28, S30, S31.3), Q2 ở S21, Q3 ở S23–S24, Q5 ở S22. Q4 (PMI) không trả lời.
